rationale:
Evidence: the only raced design (iteration 2: kp 3.0, kd 0.5, ki 0, base_speed 1.4, sensors at y 0.04, size 0.012) finished 0 of 60 trials, and every run ended off track. The oval reached 22% progress on average, the s-bend 4% and the slalom 3.5%. The s-bend and slalom scores barely vary across seeds, so those runs fail early and consistently, not after a slow drift. rms_error is small (0.025 to 0.03 m), but max_error sits at about 0.06 m, the off-track limit. The robot makes sharp excursions, most likely from over-aggressive steering at speed combined with a late line view.

Changes: (1) base_speed 1.4 to 1.2, so the robot enters bends more slowly and has more time to correct. This costs some lap time, but finishing is worth 500 points, and 1.2 still gives about 60% PWM. (2) kp 3.0 to 2.2, to reduce overshoot from strong corrections at speed. (3) kd 0.5 to 0.7, to damp the swing that a lower kp can still leave. (4) ki 0.0 to 0.1, a small integral to offset the fixed motor mismatch, with the integral bounded at plus or minus 2. (5) sensor y 0.04 to 0.06, to see the line about 2 cm further ahead and cut lag-driven overshoot. (6) sensor_size 0.012 to 0.016, so each footprint covers more of the 25 mm tape and the signal is smoother across the line. Geometry otherwise stays the same, so the race tests the controller and sensing change together.

Expected result: fewer early off-track exits, with progress well above 0.04 on the s-bend and slalom and above 0.5 on the oval. First finishes are possible but not certain, because a 1.2 base may be slow for the 3 s limit. Main risk: the lower speed and kp may run too slowly to finish in time, which the next race's completion_time will show.
